title: Mutual zugzwang and mined squares
summary: Positions where the side to move loses, and the squares a king must not step on first.
part.trebuchet.title: The trébuchet
part.trebuchet.summary: Two blocked pawns, two attacking kings: whoever has the move loses.
part.mined.title: Mined squares
part.mined.summary: The square your king must not step on first, and how to make the other king step on his.
part.race.title: Threaten before you step
part.race.summary: Attack the pawn from a safe square and force the enemy king onto the mine.
part.defend.title: The zugzwang that saves
part.defend.summary: On the weaker side, the same squares hold the draw and even set a trap.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: Two rules for your games, the technique in the mirror and the key position to play.
step.t_treb: Both pawns are blocked. Each king protects its own pawn and attacks the other one. Imagine Black to move. What happens? And with White to move?
step.t_treb.hint1: No pawn can move. Whoever has the move can only move the king.
step.t_treb.hint2: If the black king leaves c4, who protects the d5-pawn? And if the white king leaves e5, who protects d4?
step.treb: Here nobody wants to move. The d5-pawn is protected only by the black king, and the d4-pawn only by the white king. The pawns cannot move, so the side to move has to move the king, and every king move abandons its own pawn. With Black to move, the black king steps away, my king takes on d5 and stands right in front of my pawn. This is a mutual zugzwang: both sides would be in zugzwang, and only the move decides.
step.name: The same position with White to move: now I am the one who loses. The white king must leave e5, the black king takes d4 and the d5-pawn marches. This position has a name: the trébuchet. It was the catapult of medieval sieges; the French verb trébucher means to stumble. And here the one who stumbles is the one who has to move. It is also called a full-point mutual zugzwang: the side to move loses the game, not half a point.
step.d_treb: Look at the trébuchet with Black to move. I play both sides.
step.d_treb.m1: The black king has to step away. Any square abandons the d5-pawn.
step.d_treb.m2: Kxd5. The black pawn is gone, and my king stands in front of my pawn.
step.d_treb.m3: The black king tries to come back.
step.d_treb.m4: Kd6: d6 is a key square of the d4-pawn. The pawn will queen.
step.trebMove: White to play and win. Build the trébuchet with Black to move, then collect the pawn.
step.trebMove.hint: Your king must protect d4 and attack d5 at the same time. Only one square does both.
step.trebMove.done: Right. Ke5 closed the trébuchet with Black to move, and the d5-pawn fell. Any other first move would have lost the d4-pawn.
step.t_mined: This is the key position of the lesson. White to move. The pawns are blocked on d5 and d6. Your king wants to take d6, the black king wants to take d5. Which way does the white king go, and which square must it not step on?
step.t_mined.hint1: Look for the squares where the two kings would form a trébuchet around d5 and d6.
step.t_mined.hint2: White king on e6 and black king on c5: a trébuchet. Whoever reaches his square first hands the move to the other side.
step.t_mined.hint3: Do not step on e6 now. Look for another square from which your king attacks d6.
step.mines: Look at the two marked squares. If my king steps on e6 and Black answers with c5, we have a trébuchet with White to move, and I lose. If the black king steps on c5 and I answer with e6, the trébuchet is his. That is why e6 is called a mined square for the white king, and c5 for the black king: whoever steps on it first blows up. When there is only one pair of such squares, the books call them mined squares.
step.trap: See what happens if I step first: Ke6? and the black king answers Kc5. Now it is my move. My king has to leave e6, the d5-pawn falls, and Black wins. The mine was mine.
step.d_mined: The right way: attack d6 from a square that is not mined.
step.d_mined.m1: Kf6! The white king heads for e7, which also attacks d6, without stepping on e6.
step.d_mined.m2: The black king comes closer. He has not stepped on c5 yet.
step.d_mined.m3: Ke7: now the d6-pawn is attacked. Black has to protect it.
step.d_mined.m4: Only c5 protects d6 in time. The black king steps on his own mine.
step.d_mined.m5: Ke6, and now stepping here is good: the black king got there first, and the trébuchet is set with Black to move.
step.d_mined.m6: The black king has to step away and abandon d6.
step.minedMove: White to play and win. Follow Viktor's path: attack d6 without stepping on the mine first.
step.minedMove.hint: Go through f6 and e7. Step on e6 only after the black king is on c5.
step.minedMove.done: Perfect. The black king had to step on c5 to defend d6, and only then did you enter e6. Black is in zugzwang.
step.t_race: Another structure: pawns on e5 and e6, the white king on c7 and the black king on g4. White to move. Where are the mined squares, and what is the move?
step.t_race.hint1: The kings form a trébuchet around e5 and e6 with White on d6 and Black on f5.
step.t_race.hint2: Kd6 right away steps on the mine. Look for a square from which your king attacks e6 and is not mined.
step.race: The mines: d6 for the white king, f5 for the black king. If I step on d6 first, Black comes to f5 and it is my move. But from d7 my king also attacks e6, and d7 is not mined. Black has to defend the pawn, and only f5 does that. Black steps on the mine, I enter d6, and it is Black's move.
step.raceTrap: This is the mistake: Kd6? Kf5!, and White is in the trébuchet with the move. My king has to step away, and the e5-pawn falls. Here every white move except Kd7 loses.
step.d_race: Watch how Black is forced to step on f5.
step.d_race.m1: Kd7! Attacks e6 from a safe square.
step.d_race.m2: The black king defends the pawn from the only square it can: f5, his own mine.
step.d_race.m3: Kd6: now it works. The trébuchet is set and it is Black's move.
step.d_race.m4: The black king has to let go of the pawn.
step.d_race.m5: Kxe6. The e5-pawn is free, with the king beside it.
step.raceMove: White to play and win. Attack e6 without stepping on the mine.
step.raceMove.hint: Your king goes to d7. If Black does not defend e6, take it.
step.raceMove.done: Well done. Black refused to step on f5, and the e6-pawn fell at once. Had he gone to f5, you would have entered d6.
step.t_defend: Now you defend. Black is better: the black king is close to the pawns. White to move. Which is the only square that saves the draw?
step.t_defend.hint1: Look for the trébuchet around d3 and d4. Which are the two mined squares?
step.t_defend.hint2: The mines are c4 for your king and e3 for Black's. Stay next to c4 without stepping on it.
step.defend: The mines here are c4 for my king and e3 for the black king. If I step on c4 first, Black comes to e3 and I lose. So I wait on b4, right next to c4. Now the black king cannot go to e3 either: I would answer Kc4 and it would be his move. Every other move loses: Kc4 steps on the mine, and the rest leave the white king too far away to answer Ke3 with Kc4.
step.defendTrap: The mistake that looks natural: Kc4?, attacking the d4-pawn. Black answers Ke3, and it is my move in the trébuchet. My king has to abandon d3. The mine was on c4.
step.d_defend: And if Black is careless, the zugzwang changes sides.
step.d_defend.m1: Kb4! The white king waits next to the mine.
step.d_defend.m2: Black steps on e3, his own mine.
step.d_defend.m3: Kc4: the trébuchet with Black to move.
step.d_defend.m4: The black king has to abandon d4.
step.d_defend.m5: Kxd4. The defender is now the one who wins.
step.defendMove: White to play and draw. Pick the right waiting square and answer the black king.
step.defendMove.hint: Wait next to c4, without stepping on it. When the black king moves away from d4, attack the pawn.
step.defendMove.done: Excellent. After Kb4 the black king went to f3, and Kc5 attacked d4: to defend the pawn he would have to step on e3, and you would answer Kc4. Kc5 was the only move, and now you are the one playing for the win.
step.rules: Two rules to take with you. First: with blocked pawns, look for the trébuchet, the two squares where each king protects its own pawn and attacks the other. They are mined squares: whoever steps on them first loses. Second: do not step on your mine; attack the pawn from another square and force the other king onto his. And when you are worse, the same count saves you: wait next to the mine, never on it.
step.mirror: The key position in the mirror, on the e-file. The mines are now d6 for your king and f5 for Black's. The path is the mirror too: c6 and d7.
step.mirrorMove: White to play and win. The same technique on the other side of the board.
step.mirrorMove.hint: Attack e6 from d7, not from d6. Step on d6 only when the black king is on f5.
step.mirrorMove.done: That's it. Kc6, Kd7 and, only with the black king on f5, Kd6. Black is in the trébuchet with the move.
step.finish: Now play the key position to the end. Do not step on e6 too early.
ex.e08: White to play and draw. Two pairs of blocked pawns, no spare pawn moves.
ex.e08.hint: The g4 and g5 pawns cannot move. Look at the trébuchet around b5 and c5: where are the mines?
ex.e08.solution: Kd3 holds (so does Kb3). The mines are c4 for the white king and b6 for Black's. Kc4? loses: after ...Kb6 it is White's move and there is no pawn move to wait with. b6? loses too. If the black king steps on b6 first, Kc4 is the answer.
ex.e10: White to play and win. Take the pawn, then mind the mine.
ex.e10.hint: After taking on c6, the white king heads for e5. Which square around e4 and e5 is your mine?
ex.e10.solution: Kxc6, and after ...Kg4, Kd6! (Kd5? steps on the mine: ...Kf4 and it is White's move). When the black king comes to f4, Kd5 closes the trébuchet with Black to move. Every move in this line is the only one that wins.
ex.e11: White to play and win. No blocked pawns, but a mutual zugzwang is hiding here.
ex.e11.hint: With the white king on b6, the pawn on c7 and the black king on c8, the side to move misses out. Who do you want to be on move?
ex.e11.solution: Kb6! reaches that position with Black to move: ...Kd7 is the only move, and Kb7 takes the pawn to a queen. It is a mutual zugzwang: with White to move there, it would be a draw, because Kc6 is stalemate and any other move lets the black king take the pawn. Ka5, Kb5 and Ka7 only draw.
ex.e13: White to play and draw. The blocked pawns are further back, on c3 and c4.
ex.e13.hint: The trébuchet here would have your king on d4 and Black's on b3. Which of the two squares is yours?
ex.e13.solution: Kd5 holds (so does Ke4). Kd4? steps on the mine: ...Kb3 and White, to move, abandons c3. And why is there no win? After Kd5, the black king defends c4 from b5, a square that is not mined. When the defender has such a square, the mine does not decide.
key.trebuchet: Each king attacks the other's pawn, and neither can take because its own pawn is defended. The side to move has to step away, losing its pawn and the game.
key.mined: Each king has its own mine here, the square beside the enemy pawn: e6 for the white king, c5 for the black one. Whoever steps on his first walks into a trébuchet with the move and loses.
key.race: The white king attacks the black pawn from above, without stepping on the mine beside it. That way it is the black king that runs out of good squares.
key.cheeseman: Each king captures a pawn on its own wing and heads back to the centre. On the way back, whoever reaches the mined square first loses: you have to stop one square short.
history: Zugzwang is a German word meaning the compulsion to move. Pawn endings have a curious feature: positions where the side to move loses, whoever that is. This is mutual zugzwang, and it decides far more games than you might think. Its harshest form is named after a medieval weapon, the trébuchet, a kind of catapult; the French verb it comes from, trébucher, means to stumble, which is exactly what happens to the king. The idea is ancient: there are zugzwang problems in shatranj, the Arabic forerunner of chess, more than a thousand years old. Mined squares are the other side of the coin: squares your king must not step on first, because doing so hands the zugzwang to the opponent. Mark Dvoretsky, one of the greatest trainers in history, gave them a section of his endgame manual.
practice: Now the real endgame: the key position, with you to move. Remember where your mine is. Pick the time control and go.
